text:
Pause on I-audit for a complete evidence
reading of Experiment

I — Sparse n=7 parity boundary. First,
identify the research

question before looking at the answer. The
question asks whether

the fixed components create a meaningful
ordering surface, whether a

particular neighborhood provides useful
guidance on that surface, or whether

a cheaper executor is equally effective.
The sample is all

5,040 orderings, and the source artifact
is
experiments/iteration-07/results/n7_parity_landscape.csv;

iteration-14/headline_cis.csv. The
horizontal axis names the recorded

independent quantity—such as permutation
size, position, distance, or

distinct evaluations. The vertical axis
names the measured outcome—such as

accuracy, error, hit probability, regret,
correlation, or hitting time. Raw

points remain visible when their count
permits. A summary line

or bar describes those points; it does not
replace them.

A capped observation receives a censor
marker, and a sampled

landscape never pretends to be
exhaustively enumerated. The central

supports this finding: Conclusion:
evolution had no reliable advantage on

this near-zero-locality landscape. The
correct limitation is: Optimum:

1.0000 held by 14 orderings, only 0.28%;
landscape standard deviation

0.113. That limitation rules out a broader
promotional interpretation while

preserving the result actually measured.
The decision carried into the

research program is: Carry this constraint
into the next experiment

and compare methods at equal cost.
Finally, compare against the

equal-budget alternative. Generations,
repeated cache hits, and distinct

evaluations are not interchangeable. A
method earns a search-efficiency

claim only when uncertainty, evaluator
resolution, optimum density, and

evaluation cost have all been accounted
for.
